articles.headline: The Deserted Claim.
articles.text:
Up where the snow shines clear and white
On the peaks that point to the summer sky,
Up in the gulch by the evening light
I saw, as we travelled slowly by,
A claim deserted and left alone,
A shaft sunk in the mountain side,
A roofless cabin of logs rough hewn,
Where some one had labored till hope had died.

And later on, when our camp was made,
And the white tents pitched for another night,
While the pine trees wildly tossed and swayed,
In the cheerful glow of our camp-fire light,
When merry voices rang in the air,
And smiling faces flashed in and out—
I thought of the cabin, rude and bare,
Of its owner who labored in hope and doubt.

He had come, perhaps, from some eastern home
For speedy wealth, to this western clime.
And homesick, and weary, and all alone,
He had faithfully toiled for some friendly sign.
Cold moans the wind through the canon deep,
And the coyote cries the night hours drear;
There are unknown footsteps that softly creep,
No comrade to help, no loved one to cheer.

Still he dreamed, as others had done before,
As others shall do in the days to come,
Of finding wealth in unbounded store,
And joyfully bringing the treasure home;
But fortune is chary when all is told—
Her smiles are hardest on earth to gain,
And where one is favored with shining gold,
A thousand others may toil in vain.

Thus I sit and muse in the camp-fire glow,
While the welcome evening meal is spread,
And the sound of the brook comes soft and low,
And the stars shine brilliantly overhead;
For my heart is saddened, as day by day
We pass in sunshine or dripping rain,
That frequent sod-mark on our way,
A deserted, desolate mining claim.
articles.summary: Unsigned poem about an abandoned mountain mining claim.

articles.text: There is danger of a flood at Mandan as water from the Missouri is already backing up into the Heart. The river broke at Mandan yesterday, however, and what danger there is will soon be gone.
articles.summary: The Missouri River ice broke at Mandan; flood danger from backwater in the Heart River expected to pass.

articles.text: A mass of ice six miles long and frozen solid passed Glendive yesterday, floating down the Yellowstone. If in its present condition it should strike the piers of the Bismarck bridge, short work would be made of it.
articles.summary: A six-mile ice mass passed Glendive on the Yellowstone, threatening the Bismarck bridge.

articles.text: A little squib in the Mandan Pioneer to the effect that a travelling man from Bismarck was braced up against a bar and forced to warble a few select tunes to the accompaniment of six-shooters in the hands of Win Roberts and friends is creating considerable comment here. Such articles may do well enough to fill up when located in imaginary places, but they easily give a place a hard reputation even when they are as devoid of foundation as was the article above referred to. The Pioneer is assured that there was no truth in the article and for the future we hope to see no more of them.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy denies a Mandan Pioneer story that Win Roberts and friends forced a Bismarck traveling man to sing at gunpoint.

articles.text: Johnny Goodall is at the Ox Bow ranch to bring in beef cattle for slaughtering. The cattle are in splendid condition and are covered with great layers of fat. No eastern man would believe that range cattle which have not been fed a spear of hay or any grain and which have had no protection except that furnished by the buttes and coolies would be in any condition except the worst. On the other hand they are as fit for butchering as any stock-fed cattle in the States. The Refrigerator Car Company are constantly receiving orders for beef. All the cattle killed have been these range cattle and every order has given perfect satisfaction.
articles.summary: Johnny Goodall is bringing in fat range beef cattle from the Ox Bow ranch for slaughter by the Refrigerator Car Company.

articles.text: Messrs. Boice and Towers came in too late last Thursday for us to make any comment on the round-up meeting to be held here April 5. In fact, we had to take the forms off the press to insert the notice published in last week's Cow Boy. Since our last issue, however, we have spoken with a number of cattle men and there is no doubt that there will be a large turnout to the meeting. The meeting for the Bad Lands association can be thoroughly canvassed at this time and thus serve a double purpose. It is not only a privilege, but a duty of every cattle man in the Bad Lands to attend the meeting of April 5. Upon the initial meetings will depend in a great measure our future success in making this point a cattle headquarters. Every man is interested in round-up meetings for his section, and every one who attends this meeting must be made to fully appreciate the value of the Bad Lands and Territorial associations.
articles.summary: Boice and Towers brought in the notice of the April 5 round-up meeting at Medora; the paper urges every Bad Lands cattleman to attend.

articles.text: The Southeast Dakota Live Stock and Breeders' Association has been organized, with headquarters at Mitchell. Representatives were present from sixteen counties and everything points to a very successful organization. The avowed purpose of the association is to develop the quality and facilitate and encourage the raising of all kinds of live stock in Southeastern Dakota. The list of members includes most of the prominent live-stock men of Southern Dakota. Right here is the explanation of the difficulty brought forward in our last stock meeting—How to get all Dakota cattle men interested in a Territorial organization? The enthusiasm displayed at the Mitchell meeting seems to prove conclusively that the association would join with the Bad Lands and other associations to form a Territorial association. There is no need in arguing the advisability of this plan. Stock growers' interests are getting so strong in Dakota that they demand a Territorial organization so that their rights may be effectually laid before the legislature and citizens at large. Especially for the reason that considerable legislation must be passed by the Territorial legislature, it is necessary to embrace all classes of live-stock men in the Territoral organization. Of course, the raising of range cattle is unknown in Southeastern Dakota, but an interchange of views between breeders and range-stock raisers will be wonderfully beneficial to both. To a great extent the interests of both classes would be identical and the united action of such a list of men as will compose the Territorial association must have great weight in carrying a measure for the general interest of all. The territorial organization will soon be a matter of vital interest and every means should be tried to induce all cattle men of the Territory to join it. The success of the Mitchell meeting is a guarantee of the success of the larger organization.
articles.summary: Editorial: the new Southeast Dakota Live Stock and Breeders' Association at Mitchell shows a Territory-wide stockmen's association is feasible.

articles.text: We have received notice of the annual meeting of the Dawson County Live Stock Association, to be held at Glendive, April 7 and 8. All stockmen are cordially invited to attend. Business of importance will be transacted, such as appointing of foreman of round-up committees, place of round-up, etc. On the evening of the 8th there will be a grand stockmen's ball and banquet. Those wishing to join the association are requested to send in their names to the secretary, C. J. Neal, of Glendive, some time before the 8th.
articles.summary: The Dawson County Live Stock Association will meet at Glendive April 7-8, with a stockmen's ball on the 8th.

articles.text:
We want credit for items taken from this paper. We are getting tired of furnishing brains for a number of territorial papers, and if the practice is continued those papers which transgress will be dropped from our exchange list.—[Yellowstone Journal.

The above is the undiluted essence of an unspeakable gall. All the time The Journal is wishing and wanting, has it ever entered the mind of the editor that perhaps other papers want credit for their articles. Coming, as the above extract does, from a paper that stole bodily a half-column article from The Cow Boy and only changed two words, to make it apply to Miles City instead of the Bad Lands, and added a few lines at the end so that the readers of The Journal might recognize the editor's bungling work—in the face of all this we certainly desire to know if the editor wants the earth fried on both sides and served with cream gravy, or will he just take it raw if a part of the solar system is thrown in?
articles.summary: The Cow Boy answers the Yellowstone Journal's complaint about uncredited clippings by accusing it of lifting a Cow Boy article.

articles.text: The official call for the election of delegates to the Territorial Republican convention to be held at Huron, April 23, has been issued. This convention will elect two delegates and two alternates to the National Republican convention to be held in Chicago, June 3. The apportionment of delegates to the different counties has been decided and Billings county is entitled to one. As this is a matter about which our citizens have thought but little, we would suggest that some consideration be given as to who shall represent our county at the Huron convention. The Territorial central committee recommended that on Saturday, April 12, primaries be held to elect delegates to the county conventions, and that on the following Wednesday the county conventions elect delegates to the Territorial convention. Our county is as yet unorganized, but before April 12 it is hoped that some one will be appointed with authority to call the meetings. The first thing then to be done is to select a county central committee which shall hereafter have such things in charge.
articles.summary: Billings County is entitled to one delegate to the Territorial Republican convention at Huron April 23; primaries recommended for April 12.

articles.headline: SPORTING NOTES.
articles.text:
Spalding's base-ball guide for 1884 is out.

Jem Goode and Sheriff, the Prussian, will box for $1,000 a side.

The Ross-Courtney scull race takes place May 25, at Oak Point.

Jay-Eye-See and Phallas will take their spring training in Louisville.

Phil Dwyer would not sell his stables and retire from the turf for $500,000.

New professional and amateur ball clubs are being organized every day.

Base-ball players all over the country are reporting for April's preliminary practice.

Lynn, Mass., and Akron, O., will run base-ball nines on the co-operative plan this summer.

Jem Mace will start for America April 10. He hasn't any idea of tackling Sullivan, however.

The great and only base-ball manager, Dan O'Leary will manage the Cincinnati Unions this season.

The American Association clubs will travel [88,704?] miles in filling their league engagements this season.

A large number of professional oarsmen and ball-players are employed as trainers by college organizations.

Duncan C. Ross was considerably surprised last week when an amateur in Chicago named Whitmore laid him on his back after a hard struggle.

There is now no doubt but that Sullivan and Thompson will meet before three months are over. A match has been made for $5,000, each side depositing $500.

Matsada Sorakichi, the Japanese wrestler, is claimed to be the strongest man in this country at present. He is learning our style of wrestling and expects to make matches with Ross, Thompson, Bibby and McLaughlan. The Japanese style of wrestling consists in shoving the opponent out of a six-foot ring.

W. H. Edwards, president of the Cleveland Association, says: "This will be a rousing season of trotting. There is more public interest than ever. The record will go down, I think, to 2:10, possibly 2:07, or between 2:08 and 2:10 somewhere. What we want most is good square trotting and no foolishness. We are buttoning them down pretty close to that with the rules now in force."
articles.summary: Column of national sporting paragraphs (baseball, boxing, wrestling, rowing, trotting); no local news.

articles.headline: ON THE RANGE. Notice—Round-Up.
articles.text: All Bad Lands cattle men and those having any interest in a Bad Lands round-up are requested to meet here on the morning of April 5, to arrange for an annual round-up of this region.
articles.summary: Standing notice calling Bad Lands cattlemen to meet at Medora on the morning of April 5 to arrange an annual round-up.

articles.headline: Call for Bad Lands Association.
articles.text: There will be a meeting held at Little Missouri crossing, the third Monday in April (the 21st) for the purpose of forming a Bad Lands Association. All raisers of live stock are requested to attend. Upon its organization, business of much importance will come before the association and it is to the interest of every man interested in live stock to attend. The Committee.
articles.summary: Call for a meeting at Little Missouri crossing on Monday, April 21, to form a Bad Lands stock association.

articles.text:
Best American cattle are quoted at 15½c, dressed weight, in Liverpool; best sheep at 18c.

The bill granting $50,000 for the suppression of the foot and mouth disease has passed the senate. It was introduced by Senator Plumb.

The Swan Land and Cattle Company has sent to England for 200 full blooded bulls for use on their ranches.—[Cheyenne Democratic Leader.

Stock reports from the north side of the Yellowstone are very favorable. The only losses occurring so far have been from wolves. Wolves are quite numerous in that locality and have occasioned considerable loss on young cattle.—[Helena, Mon., Independent.

Out of over 8,300,000 head of live stock received at Chicago last year only 273 cattle, 758 hogs, 332 sheep and 21 calves were condemned by inspecting officers at the stock yards. This shows wonderful sanitary soundness or very poor inspection.—[Cheyenne Democratic Leader.

An exchange gives the following as a means of detecting glanders: A bucket half full of water should be held under the animal's nostrils and the mucous allowed to drop into the water. If the substance remains on top or spreads or dissolves the disease is not glanders, but if the drop remains undissolved and sinks to the bottom the horse should be killed.

A letter from north of the river says cattle are looking fine and horses doing well. The winter has not been as hard on cattle north of the river as in this vicinity. We hear of some outfits close to Sidney that have lost a good many "dogies" that were put on the range late in the fall. The railroad has not killed as many cattle as it did last year, the number on the main line between Antelope and North Platte being about two hundred and fifty.—[Sidney, Neb., Plaindealer.

The department of state has received information from the United States consul at Birmingham, Eng., that the foot and mouth disease is raging among the cattle in almost every county in England. The secretary of the treasury has requested the secretary of state to notify the United States consuls in Great Britain not to certify to invoices of cattle unless, after an examination of the animals by a veterinary surgeon, they are satisfied no disease exists.—[N. W. Live Stock Journal.

The New Mexico stock growers have requested the legislature of that territory to enact a law requiring butchers to give a bond of $1,000 to keep a record, open at all times to public inspection, containing a description of all the animals they slaughter and the names of parties from whom purchased; also to keep the hides of slaughtered animals for a reasonable length of time, thus enabling parties to identify their property. The request is a reasonable one and a law to that effect would materially aid in the detection of thieves, while a compliance with its provisions would entail no hardships on the butchers.—[N. W. Live Stock Journal.

White & Moulton, of the Lochuquilla ranch in Crockett county, are lambing 6,000 to 7,000 ewes by loose herding or line riding, with only two or three extra hands. This is no new plan, but it is very rarely practiced, especially in open range, and we know of no large ranch in Texas that has heretofore had the courage to adopt it. So far it is a success and will end successfully, from the common-sense fact that an animal left to itself will take care of its young. The only objection to the mode is the presence of wild animals, but it costs considerable less to keep a pack of good dogs and buy an ounce or two of poison than it does to put seven or eight Mexicans with each band through the lambing season. The demand is imperative for a law against wild animals. If a fair price was allowed for their scalps, the sheep's natural enemies would soon be extirpated.—[Texas Wool Grower.

Mr. John Snodgrass, general foreman of the Bay State Live Stock Company, was in town last evening and from him we learn of the purchase by the Bay State Company of the herd of John F. Coad, ranging on Pumpkin creek and the North Platte river. The price paid was $730,000 and the number of cattle given in was 23,000 head, the outfit to be run by Mr. Coad until July first when the final transfer will be made. The Bay State Company now controls about 75,000 cattle and is the second in size if not the largest in the country. It is the expectation of the company to brand about ten thousand calves this spring, the Creighton herd which was purchased last spring being largely composed of breeding stock. This company now has two ranches on the Lodge Pole, near Antelope, one on Horse creek and the Coad ranches, their range covering the western half of the county south of the river, including the heads of Pumpkin and Horse creeks and the Lodge Pole. The principal brand of the company will be the half circle block, originally the Creighton brand, and all the young stock will be branded with that brand.—[Sidney, Neb., Plaindealer-Telegraph.
articles.summary: Range news clipped from other papers: cattle prices, foot-and-mouth disease, wolves on the Yellowstone, a glanders test, a New Mexico butcher law, Texas lambing, and the Bay State Live Stock Co. purchase of the Coad herd.

articles.headline: On a Thousand Hills.
articles.text:
A. H. Swan, of Cheyenne City, is not only the cattle king of Wyoming Territory, but probably the leading cattle king in the entire West, having control of as much stock as any single individual on the continent. His present possessions amount to between $2,000,000 and $3,000,000, while the amount of stock of which he has the exclusive control and management is over 200,000 head, and valued at over $6,000,000. He was the organizer, is directly interested in and is president and general manager of no less than five different stock organizations in Wyoming, having the personal superintendency and entire management of the same. One of these cattle ranges is 100 miles in length by from 50 to 100 miles in width, and hence contains an immense acreage of grazing surface, including the best land in the territory, and lying along the Laramie, Medicine Bow, North Platte and other rivers. Beside the large amount of capital invested in stock, of which this individual has full control, some of the companies have made large purchases of land on which they have completed extensive improvements and which were done by this cattle king's suggestions and directions, so that he has the entire credit of accumulating, massing and controlling this immense congregation of wealth.

The career of this person has been remarkable for its brilliant success financially. At twenty-two years of age he travelled from his native place, Green county, Pa., to Iowa, locating in the latter state on some wild land when everything in that commonwealth was comparatively free from the intrusion of civilization. This was in 1853. At that time he had $1,000 in his pocket as his stock in trade. After making some improvements on his land he sold out at an advance, and then pushed still further on to the frontier, again investing in land. Two years after his first entrance into Iowa, he returned to Ohio, where he purchased a farm, remaining in the latter state seven years, at the end of which time he again returned to Iowa, and began dealing in sheep and cattle, buying and selling. Taking his brother as a partner they began turning their attention to the cattle business exclusively, beginning with a herd of 3,000. This herd was increased at various times as follows, naturally and purchase: In 1874 to 5,000, in 1875 to 7,000, in 1876 to 10,000, in 1877 to 11,000, in 1878 to 14,000, in 1879 to 19,000, in 1880 to 24,000, in 1881 to 28,000 and in 1882 to [33,000?]. Most of the increase was natural.

By this time the profits of the two brothers in the stock business had been so great, not including the stock on hand, that the next year (1883), with several other stockmen they purchased 31,000 more cattle on a range west of the Black Hills, merging their two herds into one, and with other parties forming a land and cattle syndicate company, with an invested capital of $2,555,000, A. H. Swan being made president of the same at a salary of $10,000 per year, the amount of cattle numbering 115,000. Negotiations are now pending for the sale of Mr. A. H. Swan's interest in this company at the princely sum of $750,000. Mr. Swan next organized four other companies on a similar basis, to all of which he has been given the direct management. One of the companies, known as the Ogallala Land and Cattle Company of Nebraska, owns 85,000 head of cattle. The latest enterprise in which this cattle king has been engaged was the organization of a land syndicate and stock yards company, which purchased 2,000 acres of land adjoining the city of Omaha, Neb., a portion to be sold in lots and the balance to be reserved for this land syndicate and stock yards company for the slaughtering and shipping of dressed beef in refrigerator cars to eastern markets. This latter establishment is to be ready for operation by July, 1884, and its capacities are placed at 1,000 head per day. Among the cattle king's private possessions are 150,000 acres of land under fence, with ten houses, eight barns and fifty corrals for the branding of stock. He is also the owner of land in Iowa, forty miles from Des Moines, valued at $350,000.

He claims to have never had any litigations about contracts, never having forfeited his word to any person with whom he has had any business transactions, either in buying or selling. In appearance he is tall, but well proportioned and his countenance bears the imprint of modesty, frankness and intelligence, and though naturally easy in his bearing, yet he is free from the suavity and independence of action so common among frontier stockmen.—[Pioneer-Press.
articles.summary: Clipped Pioneer-Press profile of Wyoming cattle king A. H. Swan and his companies.

articles.text:
A Mr. Terry, of England, has invented a tricycle which is capable of being converted into a boat. When used on the road the machine is an ordinary rear steerer. The operation of converting it into a boat is very simple and takes but half an hour. All mounted, the apparatus forms a decked canoe, combining all the conditions necessary for proper buoyancy, even at sea. The buoyancy is, moreover, increased by two air bags, which are attached to the two sides at the upper part of the open space.—[Mirror of American Sports.

Woodside and Morgan on May 1 will start on their trans-continental bicycle trip from New York to San Francisco. Two thousand dollars is up that they will cover the distance in seventy days.

At last the names of the St. Paul nine have been published. It is long odds that they will bring up the rear in the Northwestern League race.
articles.summary: Clipped sporting miscellany: a convertible tricycle-boat, a planned transcontinental bicycle trip, and the St. Paul baseball nine.

articles.text: Dr. A. R. Duncan, surgeon of the N. P. R. R., and H. S. Davis, both of Glendive, made us a call last Friday. It is probable that Dr. Duncan will arrange for weekly visits here.

articles.text: A number of the boys are interested in base-ball and practice daily for a while after dinner. A nine will be organized soon, which will result in considerable sport, if not in glory.
articles.summary: Local young men practice baseball daily; a nine is to be organized.

articles.text: It is the unanimous opinion of men here from all parts of the world, that they have never experienced more delightful weather than we are having at present. It is simply perfect.
articles.summary: Weather reported as perfect.

articles.text: Jos. Doulisch, an account of whose accident we published in our last issue, is rapidly recovering. It was feared for a time that his pelvis was injured, but his rapid recovery contradicts that idea.
articles.summary: Jos. Doulisch is recovering from the accident reported last week.

articles.text: Adolph Eyraud, the Marquis' gardener, is hard at work on his garden, getting hot-beds in order. Owing to this being the first year, there are many difficulties to overcome, but Mr. Eyraud's hopes are high.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Morès' gardener Adolph Eyraud is preparing hot-beds for his first season.

articles.text: Considerable sport has been had here lately over a number of races. Several of the ponies have exhibited extraordinary speed at two hundred yards, but none can take away the championship for that distance from "Old Tex."
articles.summary: Pony races at Medora; "Old Tex" keeps the 200-yard championship.

articles.text: The bears are a great curiosity and are let loose occasionally for the delectation of passengers on the cars. The bears always take a shoot for the dining-car and their confidence is usually rewarded by a liberal donation of scraps.

articles.text: Mr. B. Barr has returned from J. A. Beaumont's sheep ranch and reports that all danger of further deaths is at an end. articles.headline: THE LAST SQUAWK Of the Dickinson Dying Duck Reminds Us of the Man Who Never Opened His Mouth, but He Put His FOOT INTO IT.
articles.text:
The last issue of The Dickinson Press was a chromo edition. It was intended to reassure its readers in reference to the Dickinson freight route, but as the bald-headed facts were known there as well as here, it must have utterly failed in its intention. The editor of The Press, however, was astute enough to put two and two together and reasoned that his chromo edition was the last or next to the last time he could hold even a bob-tail straight in his bluff game and so he went his whole stack on the last deal. At least, the above is the explanation we received from a friend. We like facts, in fact, we are stuck on them, so we packed our spare suit in a handker—grip, we mean—and started for Dickinson last Friday, bound to know something more than hearsay about the merits of the two routes. We found Dickinson to be a lively, bustling place, very well calculated to predispose anyone in its favor. In company with a friend we rode out several miles on the proposed Dickinson route. The ground was frozen so that it was hard to judge of the nature of the soil, but there was considerable gumbo grass and frequent indications of quicksand. The country was rolling, but the first few miles of the route are level enough, with the exception of one steep hill. We very much doubt, however, if the gumbo will be passable during wet weather. In fact, several of the Dickinson citizens admitted as much. It must be borne in mind also that this is the best part of the Dickinson route.

The next day, in company with Messrs. Keyes, Pennell and Hyde, we took a long trip over the Medora route. It must also be remembered that right here in the Bad Lands is the only poor part of our route. Outside of the Bad Lands, every one unites in saying that there is not a more perfect route in the country. In the Bad Lands it is, on the whole, more level than the Dickinson route but there are more hills. Only the Sully creek hill would compel teams to double, however, and the bridge does away entirely with this difficulty.

Summing up, we believe the first twenty-five miles of the Dickinson route is preferable to ours, if the gumbo can be avoided. Otherwise our twenty-five miles in the Bad Lands are vastly preferable. For the remaining hundred and sixty miles, there is no question but that our route is far superior.

As the matter has gone beyond argument now and the success of our route is assured, there is no need of mentioning these facts.

Whether there is to be a route from Dickinson or not, we neither know nor care. What we do know is that contracts have been signed with Black Hills merchants for the hauling of their freight that will test the four hundred teams on our route to the utmost.

Up to the date of the publication of the chromo edition, not a merchant had made a contract specifying that his goods were to be shipped by the Dickinson route. Not a contractor had decided to ship via Dickinson. Not a stroke of work had been done on their route. And oh, tempora, the route hadn't even been "viewed" by the enterprising committee appointed for that purpose.
articles.summary: Packard reports riding out the rival Dickinson freight route last Friday and the Medora route the next day with Keyes, Pennell and Hyde, and declares the Medora-Black Hills route superior and assured.

articles.headline: BELFIELD GOSSIP.
articles.text:
Belfield, Dak., March 26, 1884.
Editor Cow Boy:

Louis C. Hay, the Grand Guy of the Belfield Townsite Company, returned home Saturday morning. Louis spent several months in New York and Washington in behalf of our town, and comes back to us the Boomer, of Boomerville. In the language of our lamented chum Napoleon, "There is music in the air."

Sheriff Cuskelly came up from Dickinson to replevin the pony which an Indian claimed was stolen from him several years before J. Christ's, Esq., birthday. As the Indian had the trademark and the sheriff on his side, the animal was turned over to him in the presence of the whole town and tears have flowed freely since. Moral—Don't buy or steal an animal with a trademark.

Bill Tuttle, the manager of the Gallien ranch in the Bad Lands, is hot and liable to crawl upon the paper collar of a couple of noble red men, who stole two valuable horses from him. It appears Bill befriended these men, who sought food and shelter at his place. After enjoying the most liberal hospitality, these copper-colored knights of the lasso departed during Mr. Tuttle's absence in town, taking along a couple of ropes on the ends of which these two horses unfortunately happened to be appended. Should they be sighted a mineral claim will be located on both of them.

Breaking and seeding will commence this week and a fine crop is surely expected.

Three men fainted dead away when The Dickinson Press reached here last week. They mistook the sickly rooster for the editor-in-chief of The Press.

Mr. Gilchrist, our end-man who keepeth watch during the darkest hour of night at the depot, has left us to accept a more lucrative position at Sully Springs. All the girls in town are praying that he will follow the valuable example of Hamlet's ghost and semi-occasionally return—when the spirit moves him, so to speak.

A. Goodrow represents Wisconsin and the night operator all at the same time at this point. He seems to be a clever boy, though the atmosphere got very dry since his arrival here.

Mr. W. M. LeMoyne, of the Belfield Townsite Company, came in Tuesday morning.

Several new bridges and houses are going up and everything indicates that the spring poet should have his life insured, if he would venture upon these pastures green.

Mine host Bass is spending a small fortune, with the accent on the first syllable, in paint and oil and in getting plans made for an addition to his popular hotel. Verily, the world moveth.

Your correspondent does not venture to church often and only when "Mamma dear" threatens to envelope us with a new bonnet. Such was the case last Sunday, and the sermon ran as follows: "And it came to pass in the year of our Lord eighteen hundred and eighty-four that some good merchants from a far away country called the Black Hills got lost in a town called Dickinson. And upon their arrival the people gathered around them and looked at each other and in silence spake, 'Blessed be those who strike Dickinson, for they will see the way to the Black Hills.' But, alas, the freighters got frightened, for the crowd's manners were wild and the spokesman had not wherewith to grease the wheel. They got. And upon their journey toward the setting sun they struck two places, recorded in the great book of the Northern Pacific as Belfield and Medora, and here the merchants seemed full of hope, faith and charity. They took kindly to the people of that locality, who slaughtered the fattest rooster in their behalf, and immediately decided upon these points for their journey home. And it is recorded in the archives, more commonly known as Scott's Dickinson Press that the fine words, 'Gold and silver have I none, but such as I have I will give thee,' are quoted superlatively N. G.
Sadie.
articles.summary: Belfield correspondent "Sadie" reports Louis C. Hay's return, a sheriff's replevin of an Indian's pony, the theft of two horses from Bill Tuttle of the Gallien ranch, Bass's hotel addition, and jibes at Dickinson.

articles.text: Mr. E. Hemple, of the Chicago firm of Oberne, Hosick & Co., has bought the hides at the abattoir here for his house. The price paid is in the neighborhood of $20,000. A dozen men are busy in cleaning and packing them. Mr. Hemple says it is the finest lot of hides he has ever purchased, and is highly complimentary to Mr. Hyde in his remarks about their good condition. A far less percentage than usual has been cut and they are all now in perfect condition. This sale makes between $25,000 and $30,000 worth of hides sold by the company since last December.
articles.summary: E. Hemple of Oberne, Hosick & Co., Chicago, bought the Medora abattoir's hides for about $20,000.

events.date_basis: Undated item in Belfield letter of Wed 26 Mar 1884
events.title: Sheriff Cuskelly turns over a pony to an Indian claimant at Belfield
events.summary: Sheriff Cuskelly came from Dickinson to replevin a pony an Indian said had been stolen from him years before; it was turned over to him before the whole town.
events.excerpt: As the Indian had the trademark and the sheriff on his side, the animal was turned over to him in the presence of the whole town

events.date_basis: Undated item in Belfield letter of Wed 26 Mar 1884
events.title: Two horses stolen from Bill Tuttle of the Gallien ranch
events.summary: Bill Tuttle, manager of the Gallien ranch in the Bad Lands, had two valuable horses taken by two Indian men he had fed and sheltered, who left while he was in town.
events.excerpt: these copper-colored knights of the lasso departed during Mr. Tuttle's absence in town

events.date_basis: Undated item in Belfield letter of Wed 26 Mar 1884
events.title: Belfield depot man Gilchrist leaves for Sully Springs
events.summary: Mr. Gilchrist, the night man at the Belfield depot, left for a better-paying position at Sully Springs; A. Goodrow was now night operator.
events.excerpt: has left us to accept a more lucrative position at Sully Springs.

events.date_basis: Undated item in Belfield letter of Wed 26 Mar 1884
events.title: Bass plans addition to his Belfield hotel
events.summary: Belfield hotel keeper Bass was painting and having plans drawn for an addition to his hotel; new bridges and houses were also going up in Belfield.
events.excerpt: in getting plans made for an addition to his popular hotel.

events.date_basis: No date given; week before Thu 27 Mar 1884 issue
events.title: E. Hemple buys the Medora abattoir's hides
events.summary: E. Hemple of Oberne, Hosick & Co. of Chicago bought the hides at the Medora abattoir for about $20,000, praising Mr. Hyde for their condition; the company's hide sales since December reached $25,000-$30,000.
events.excerpt: The price paid is in the neighborhood of $20,000.
